title: tenant-throttling-simulator-and-parameterization-guide-2026
author: Aisha Coleman
content:
Summary:
This guide describes the Tenant Throttling Simulator (TTS): a reproducible experiment harness for exploring throttling and eviction policy parameterizations across multitenant inference workloads. TTS is intended for platform engineers who must make data-driven choices for tenant rate limits, priority slices, and eviction heuristics that balance SLO attainment, fairness, and cost.

Problem statement and motivation:
- At scale, small changes to per-tenant throttles or eviction thresholds can produce large, non-linear effects on latency SLOs and tail cost.
- We lack a repeatable way to run parameter sweeps that combine realistic arrival patterns, KV cache statefulness, and cross-region failover scenarios.
- The simulator gives operators a way to (a) quantify SLO vs cost tradeoffs, (b) stress-test fairness under skewed tenant distributions, and (c) generate rollout safe-ranges for production configuration.

Scope and audience:
- Audience: platform operators, SREs, runtime engineers, and product owners who own tenant-level economics.
- Scope: local and cluster-scale simulation of request routing, batching, KV-prefix cache hit-rate dynamics, and admission control. Not in scope: full model inference latency micro-benchmarks (those belong in eng-serving-runtime).

High-level architecture (textual diagram):
- Driver (experiment runner): orchestrates scenarios and parameter sweeps.
- Synthetic workload generator: tenant arrival distributions, request size histogram, interactive vs batch mix.
- Runtime model: simplified per-GPU queuing model + batch formation + kv-prefix cache layer + eviction/admission logic.
- Metrics collector: computes SLO attainment, p50/p95/p99 latencies, tokens-per-second, and cost proxy.
- Analyzer: generates heatmaps, Pareto frontiers, and recommended parameter ranges.

Key concepts and knobs:
- tenant_throttle (rpm): per-tenant request-per-minute soft cap applied before batching.
- priority_slice: integer tier (0..N) controlling burst credits and admission precedence.
- eviction_policy: {LRU, LFU, TTL-weighted, recency+size} for KV prefix cache.
- admission_margin: float [0.0, 1.0], portion of capacity reserved for SLO-critical traffic.
- batch_window_ms: batching delay budget used to assemble batches (affects throughput vs latency).

Representative experiment matrix (table):
| Experiment ID | tenant skew | tenant_throttle | priority_slice distribution | eviction_policy | admission_margin | notes |
| E-101 | even (N=200) | 30 rpm | {gold:5%,silver:15%,bronze:80%} | LRU | 0.1 | baseline |
| E-203 | skewed (90/10) | 10 rpm for tail | {gold:2%,silver:8%,bronze:90%} | TTL-weighted | 0.25 | high-skew stress |
| E-311 | enterprise burst | 200 rpm burst | {gold:50%,silver:30%,bronze:20%} | recency+size | 0.0 | burst credit sizing |

Inputs required for a run:
- tenant manifest (CSV): tenant_id, class (gold/silver/bronze), baseline_rps, burst_profile_id
- arrival profile (JSON): Poisson/zipf parameters, diurnal window, synthetic outage window
- runtime config (YAML): admission_margin, batch_window_ms, throttle_map, eviction_policy params

Quick start (local):
1) Clone the simulator repository (private/internal): git clone git@redwood:platform/tenant-throttling-sim.git && cd tenant-throttling-sim
2) Create a scenario: cp scenarios/example-scenario.yaml scenarios/your-test.yaml and edit tenant counts and skew
3) Run a single-point experiment: ./bin/run_experiment --scenario scenarios/your-test.yaml --out results/exp-your-test.json
4) Produce a dashboard-style summary (local): ./bin/analyze --input results/exp-your-test.json --format html --out results/exp-your-test.html

Parallel parameter sweep (cluster):
- The driver supports Kubernetes Job fanout: use k8s template jobs/sim-job.yaml and a param generator to map sweep dimensions to jobs.
- Tip: limit parallelism to 40 jobs to avoid overloading shared telemetry backends during analysis.

Interpreting outputs and recommended thresholds:
- SLO attainment: primary metric is p95 latency <= configured SLO for SLO-critical tenant classes. If p95 breach > 5% of time windows, mark config as risky.
- Fairness score: normalized ratio of p95 between gold and bronze (target < 2.0 to avoid extreme disparity).
- Cost-proxy: tokens-per-second / effective_gpu_utilization. Use increase over baseline to estimate incremental cost.

Decision matrix (example):
- If SLO attainment for gold < 99.5% and fairness score > 2.5 -> increase admission_margin by +0.1 and reduce batch_window_ms by 10ms.
- If cost-proxy increases > 15% but SLOs remain good -> consider tightening throttle for bronze by 10% and increasing eviction aggressiveness.
- If KV cache hit-rate < 40% for high-volume tenants -> prefer recency+size eviction and increase cache hot-shard allocation.

Production rollout runbook (safe rollout pattern):
1) Canary: apply new parameter set to a small isolated shard (1% of traffic) for 24h. Monitor p50/p95/p99, token-cost, and error rates.
2) Gradual ramp: 5% -> 20% -> 50% over 3–7 days with automated abort if p95 breach > 2% in any window.
3) Fallback: pre-provision and keep previous config snapshot; automated fallback job will restore previous admission_margin and throttle_map if rollback triggered.
4) Post-rollout review: publish experiment artifacts and a short findings note to the runbook.

Operational alerting guidance (dashboards and alerts):
- Create a synthetic SLO monitor for representative tenants per class; alert when p95(SLO-class) breaches target for 3 consecutive windows of 1 minute.
- Cost drift alert: when cost-proxy delta > 12% sustained for 30 minutes.
- Fairness regression alert: when fairness score change > 0.5 in 1 hour.

Experiment reproducibility checklist:
- Commit scenario YAML and driver version (git SHA) into artifacts directory.
- Include seed values for RNGs to ensure identical arrival traces.
- Archive any telemetry dumps required for offline replay.

Common pitfalls and mitigations:
- Pitfall: mixing synthetic and production traces without normalization -> Mitigation: use normalization layer that rescales arrival rates to match target qps.
- Pitfall: ignoring KV cache warmup -> Mitigation: run warmup phase for at least 2x median TTL before measurement window.
- Pitfall: telemetry overload during large sweeps -> Mitigation: aggregate at driver and emit summarized metrics rather than full traces.

Ownership, responsibilities and SLAs:
- Owner: Platform/Serving Capacity team (primary), Eng-SRE (secondary). Contact: platform-eng@redwood.internal
- SLA for experiment infrastructure: driver availability 99.9% during business hours.

Retrospective and continuous improvement notes (how to use results):
- Store the Pareto frontier (SLO vs cost) from each major sweep in the experiment catalog.
- Quarterly review: re-run E-101 baseline against latest traffic shapes; identify drift in recommended admission_margin.

Appendix: sample runtime-config YAML snippet:
```yaml
admission_margin: 0.15
batch_window_ms: 30
throttle_map:
  gold: 60
  silver: 30
  bronze: 10
eviction_policy:
  name: recency+size
  max_entry_size_kb: 64
  recency_weight: 0.7
  size_weight: 0.3
```

Appendix: example CLI invocation for cluster sweep (k8s):
- python tools/param_sweeper.py --param admission_margin:0.0,0.1,0.2 --param eviction_policy:name:LRU,recency+size --parallel 20 --out s3://redwood-experiments/2026-ttsim/

Notes and references:
- This doc is intentionally pragmatic: it links simulator outputs to rollout steps and alerting. For microbenchmarking guidance see eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling.
- If you use this harness for customer-impacting changes (tenant-visible throttles or burst credits), include Security and Compliance in the review cycle.

Contact and feedback:
- Open an RFC (platform/experiments) if you want new knobs added to the simulator. For urgent help during rollouts, ping #platform-ops on Slack or email platform-eng@redwood.internal.
